nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-031.prompt: A novice’s knees cave inward at the bottom of a bodyweight squat. You cue “knees out.” What is that cue meant to produce?

options.a: Knees tracking over the feet instead of collapsing into valgus
options.b: Knees shoved well past the little toes into extra hip turnout
options.c: Knees locked behind the toes no matter how the torso leans
options.d: Weight shifted onto the balls of the feet so they can sit deeper

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-031.explanation: “Knees out” is a tracking cue: the knees should follow the line of the feet so the hip, knee, and foot stay stacked. It is not a rule against forward knee travel and not a cue to spin the knees outside the fifth toe. Valgus collapse is the fault; mid-foot balance stays the goal.

distractorExplanations.b: Forcing the knees outside the little toes over-rotates the hips and can stress the knee rather than restore tracking.
distractorExplanations.c: Forward knee travel can be normal; the cue is medial-lateral tracking, not keeping knees behind the toes.
distractorExplanations.d: Shifting onto the toes is a balance fault; the squat should stay over the mid-foot while the knees track.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-032.prompt: You set a novice for a conventional deadlift from the floor. Which start position is the best default?

options.a: Hips as low as a squat, bar over the toes, and weight on the forefoot
options.b: Neutral spine, bar over mid-foot, shoulders slightly ahead of the bar
options.c: Rounded upper back, heels lifted, and the bar hovering in front of the toes
options.d: Shoulders behind the bar, chest high, and heels raised off the floor

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-032.explanation: A conventional deadlift starts with a braced, relatively neutral spine, the bar over the mid-foot, and the shoulders over or slightly in front of the bar so the lats can keep the bar close. It is a hinge-pull, not a squat with the bar out over the toes, and the feet stay flat.

distractorExplanations.a: Squat-depth hips push the knees forward and the bar off mid-foot, turning the first pull into a squat-yank.
distractorExplanations.c: A rounded start loads the spine in flexion, and raised heels dump weight onto the toes.
distractorExplanations.d: Shoulders behind the bar and raised heels both move the bar path forward of the mid-foot.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-033.prompt: A client is bench-pressing a hard set of five. How should you spot the barbell bench press?

options.a: Lift through every concentric so the bar never slows or stalls
options.b: Stand beside the bench and spot the lift by holding the elbows
options.c: Stay at the head of the bench; help unrack and assist only if the bar stalls
options.d: Stand several steps back and step in only after a failed press attempt

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-033.explanation: A bench spotter stands at the head of the bench with a mixed or alternated grip ready on the bar, helps with a controlled unrack/hand-off, and assists only if the bar stalls or the lifter asks. Lifting every rep removes the training stimulus; an elbow-side spot or a late step-in cannot control a falling bar.

distractorExplanations.a: Assisting every rep turns the set into a partner lift and hides true sticking points.
distractorExplanations.b: Elbow spotting cannot control a loaded bar over the face; hands belong on the bar at the head of the bench.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting until after a miss is too late; the spotter stays close enough to take the bar immediately.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-034.prompt: Box-jump landings show the client’s knees collapsing into valgus. What should you do first?

options.a: Raise the box so they have to absorb more landing force next
options.b: Add a loaded trap-bar jump so the hips have to work harder
options.c: Cue the knees inward so they can “absorb” the landing better
options.d: Cue knees over toes and hips back, or regress the box height

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-034.explanation: Valgus on landing is a control problem, not a reason to add height or load. Cue knee tracking over the feet with hips back, and drop the box or switch to a lower-impact landing drill until the pattern is stable. Loading a collapsing landing raises knee stress.

distractorExplanations.a: More height increases landing force on a pattern that is already failing.
distractorExplanations.b: Adding external load on a valgus landing raises joint stress before control is restored.
distractorExplanations.c: Knees caving inward is the valgus fault itself; the cue is knees over the feet, not in.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-035.prompt: You want hinge work without a dead-stop from the floor. Why choose a Romanian deadlift over a conventional deadlift?

options.a: The RDL is a standing hip hinge with less knee bend and no floor start
options.b: The RDL uses more knee bend and a squat-style pull from the plates
options.c: The RDL starts each rep from a dead stop on the floor like a conventional pull
options.d: The RDL needs a snatch-width grip and a fully vertical torso

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-035.explanation: The RDL starts from standing and lowers the bar with a hip hinge and soft knees, typically to mid-shin, then returns by hip extension. Conventional deadlifts start from the floor with more knee bend. Grip width is similar to a conventional pull, and the torso leans as the hips travel back.

distractorExplanations.b: More knee bend and a floor pull describe the conventional deadlift, not the RDL.
distractorExplanations.c: Starting from the floor each rep is the conventional deadlift; the RDL never parks the bar.
distractorExplanations.d: A snatch grip and upright torso are Olympic-lift setup ideas, not RDL mechanics.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-036.prompt: A client is holding a front plank. When should you end the set as a technique fail?

options.a: When breathing under the brace becomes audible or heavy
options.b: When the hips pike or sag past the body line you cued
options.c: When the stopwatch hits the 60-second target you wrote
options.d: When the legs and trunk begin to tremble slightly

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-036.explanation: A plank is a position, not a clock. The set ends when the client can no longer hold a roughly straight line from head to heels—hips sagging into lumbar extension or piking up. Mild shake and heavier breathing are fatigue, not automatic failure; time is only a target if the position is still honest.

distractorExplanations.a: Steady or heavier breathing while the brace holds is expected; position loss is the fail.
distractorExplanations.c: Hitting a time goal with a broken line still counts as a failed plank; stop when the line goes.
distractorExplanations.d: Mild trembling is common fatigue; failure is the hips leaving the cued line.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-037.prompt: A client overhead-presses by flinging the ribs into a large lumbar arch to finish each rep. What should you cue?

options.a: A deeper lumbar arch so the bar can clear the face more easily
options.b: Behind-the-neck pressing so beginners can shorten the bar path more
options.c: Ribs down and a stacked torso so the bar finishes over the mid-foot
options.d: Scapulae locked down with no upward rotation through the whole press

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-037.explanation: Overhead pressing needs a braced, stacked ribcage over the pelvis so the bar finishes over the mid-foot without a giant lumbar dump. The head can pull back slightly to clear the bar; the low back should not become the path. Scapulae must upwardly rotate, and behind-the-neck pressing is a poor default for limited shoulders.

distractorExplanations.a: A bigger arch shifts load onto the lumbar spine instead of finishing the press with the shoulders.
distractorExplanations.b: Behind-the-neck pressing demands extreme external rotation and is not a beginner default.
distractorExplanations.d: Locking the blades down blocks scapular upward rotation and can impinge the shoulder.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-038.prompt: On a bent-over barbell row, the client’s torso pops up and the bar swings into the hips. What is the primary fault?

options.a: The grip is too narrow to let the elbows travel back
options.b: The elbows are tracking too close to the ribcage
options.c: The load is too light for the lats to feel the row
options.d: They are using hip drive and losing the hinged torso

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-038.explanation: A bent-over row keeps a stable hip hinge while the arms pull the bar to the torso. If the torso rises and the bar swings, the client is turning the row into a hip-hinge cheat. Cue a quieter torso, a closer bar path, and usually a lighter load—not a narrower grip or more weight.

distractorExplanations.a: Grip width is a secondary setup choice; the visible fault is the lost hinge, not a narrow grip.
distractorExplanations.b: Elbows near the ribs can be a valid row path; it does not explain a rising torso and swinging bar.
distractorExplanations.c: Too much load, not too little, usually causes the torso to pop and the bar to swing.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-039.prompt: A client’s kettlebell swing looks like a squat plus a front raise. Which pattern should you restore?

options.a: A hip-hinge power snap with the arms only guiding the bell
options.b: A squat-dominant jump that parks the bell at eye level
options.c: A shoulder-driven raise that lifts the bell with the delts
options.d: A spinal-flexion crunch that loads the low back on purpose

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-039.explanation: The swing is a fast hip hinge: the hips load back, then snap to extension while the arms stay long as a tether. Squatting the bell and lifting it with the shoulders turns it into a front raise. The spine stays braced and neutral; it is not a flexion-based core drill.

distractorExplanations.b: A squat-dominant swing dumps the knees forward and usually floats the bell with the arms.
distractorExplanations.c: The delts do not lift the bell; they only keep the arms long while the hips supply power.
distractorExplanations.d: Spinal flexion under a swinging load is a fault, not a core strategy.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-040.prompt: Mid-set, a client’s squat bar drifts forward of the mid-foot. What does that usually mean?

options.a: They need more forward torso lean so they can sit back
options.b: They are losing mid-foot balance toward the toes
options.c: The bar is simply placed too low on the upper back
options.d: They are sitting too far onto the heels and pulling the bar back

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-040.explanation: The bar should stay over the mid-foot. Forward drift usually means the center of mass has shifted onto the toes—chest falling, heels light, or knees shooting forward without control. Cue mid-foot pressure and a quieter bar path, and drop load if the pattern stays ugly. Extra lean or blaming low-bar placement misses the balance fault.

distractorExplanations.a: More forward lean moves the bar farther in front of the mid-foot, worsening the drift.
distractorExplanations.c: Low-bar placement can increase torso lean but still keeps the bar over mid-foot if balance is good.
distractorExplanations.d: Sitting onto the heels pulls the bar backward; forward drift is the opposite weight shift.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-041.prompt: A rear-foot-elevated split squat wobbles so much that the front knee hunts side to side. What should you do?

options.a: Hand them dumbbells so extra load is said to “increase stability”
options.b: Lengthen the stance and slow the eccentric to demand more control
options.c: Shorten the stance or let them hold a support, then add load later
options.d: Progress to a single-leg box jump to train that same balance demand

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-041.explanation: A split squat that cannot be balanced is too hard. Shorten the stance, lower the rear-foot elevation, or let the client hold a rack or dowel until the front knee tracks. Load and plyometrics wait until the pattern is quiet. Extra mass and a longer stance both raise the balance demand.

distractorExplanations.a: Dumbbells magnify an unstable base; load is added after the stance is controlled.
distractorExplanations.b: A longer stance increases mobility and balance demand, the opposite of a regression.
distractorExplanations.d: A box jump is a harder plyometric task, not a fix for an unstable split squat.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-042.prompt: For a heavy working-set squat, which breathing strategy is the usual coaching default?

options.a: Exhale throughout the descent so the trunk stays relaxed under load
options.b: Inhale during the ascent right at the sticking point of the squat
options.c: Take rapid shallow breaths on every inch of the repetition
options.d: Brace the trunk (Valsalva as appropriate) before the descent

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-042.explanation: Heavy squats need a stiff trunk. The usual cue is a breath in, a brace (Valsalva when appropriate for a healthy client), then descent and drive before a controlled exhale at or after lockout. Exhaling on the way down or panting through the rep dumps intra-abdominal pressure when the spine needs it most.

distractorExplanations.a: Exhaling on the descent loses trunk stiffness under the heaviest part of the squat.
distractorExplanations.b: Inhaling at the sticking point breaks the brace exactly when the bar is hardest to move.
distractorExplanations.c: Shallow panting never creates a usable brace; it is a fatigue pattern, not a cue.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-043.prompt: A deconditioned novice cannot keep a goblet squat over mid-foot without the knees caving. When is a machine squat or leg press the better next step?

options.a: Never; free-weight squats must start on session one no matter the collapse
options.b: When you need a safer load while you rebuild the squat pattern
options.c: When you want to skip teaching any squat or hinge pattern at all
options.d: Only for competitive lifters who already squat well without a guide

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-043.explanation: Machines are a tool, not a cop-out. If free-weight balance or valgus is the limiter, a guided squat or leg press can load the legs while you coach the pattern with lighter goblet or box squats. They do not replace movement teaching, and they are often most useful for novices—not only for skilled competitive lifters.

distractorExplanations.a: Forcing free weights on day one with a collapsing squat is a technique and safety error.
distractorExplanations.c: Machines can load the legs, but the CPT still teaches a squat or hinge the client can own.
distractorExplanations.d: Guided loading is often more useful for unstable novices than for already-skilled lifters.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-044.prompt: A client wants a heavy lat pulldown and has limited shoulder external rotation. Which version should you choose?

options.a: Behind-the-neck pulldowns despite the tight shoulders and limited rotation
options.b: A max-load pulldown with a bounce off the upper chest each rep
options.c: A controlled pulldown to the upper chest with the bar in front
options.d: A kipping pull-up so extra momentum replaces scapular control

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-044.explanation: A front pulldown to the upper chest keeps the humerus in a friendlier path and lets you control scapular depression and elbow drive. Behind-the-neck pulldowns demand more external rotation than this client has. Momentum and chest-bounce loading hide the very control the CPT is trying to teach.

distractorExplanations.a: Behind-the-neck pulling plus limited external rotation is a classic shoulder-stress setup.
distractorExplanations.b: Bouncing the bar off the chest trades control for load and is not a technique upgrade.
distractorExplanations.d: Kipping uses extra body swing; it does not teach a controlled vertical pull for this client.

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-045.prompt: A client’s lumbar spine rounds as a conventional deadlift leaves the floor. What should you do on the next attempt?

options.a: Cue more speed so they yank past the sticky start position
options.b: Drop the hips into a squat so the knees start well in front of the bar
options.c: Add a hitch at the knees to grind the lockout after the round
options.d: Lower the load and reset a braced spine with the bar over mid-foot

nsca-cpt-readiness-check-technique-045.explanation: Lumbar flexion under load is a stop-and-reset fault, not a cue to pull faster. Drop the weight, rebuild a braced neutral start, and keep the bar over the mid-foot. Speed, extra knee bend, or hitching a rounded spine all train the same problem at a higher risk.

distractorExplanations.a: Yanking faster with a rounded lumbar spine increases spinal loading, it does not fix the start.
distractorExplanations.b: Squatting the hips lower pushes the knees forward and the bar off mid-foot; that is not a back-set fix.
distractorExplanations.c: A hitch after rounding rewards a broken pattern instead of resetting the brace.
